question: What is the difference between population variance and sample variance?
answer: The key difference between population variance and sample variance is the denominator used in their calculations. [S3] Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by N, the population size [S1]. Sample variance, used when data are a sample used to estimate a larger population, divides by n - 1 [S1] [S2].

citations.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
citations.text:
1. Bias of an Estimator
In statistics the bias of an estimator is its expected value minus the true parameter it estimates. An
estimator with zero bias is called unbiased. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the
population mean. The sample variance that divides by n - 1 is an unbiased estimator of the
population variance, while dividing by n gives a biased estimator that underestimates the
population variance by the factor (n - 1) / n.
Estimator bias is a property of a calculation procedure over repeated samples. It is different from
sampling bias, which is a flaw in how the data were collected, for example surveying only
volunteers.

citations.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
citations.text:
Problem 1: Sample versus Population Variance
Question. For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 compute the population variance and the sample variance.
Solution. The mean is 40 / 8 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. The population variance is 32 / 8 = 4 and the population standard deviation is 2. Treated as a sample, the sample variance is 32 / 7, about 4.571, and the sample standard deviation is about 2.138. The sample version is larger because it divides by n - 1 instead of n.

S4.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
S4.text:
2. Variance of an Estimator
The variance of an estimator describes how much the estimate changes from one random sample
to the next. For the sample mean it equals sigma squared divided by n, so the standard error of the
mean is sigma divided by the square root of n.
This is not the same quantity as the variance of the data themselves, which describes the spread
of individual observations around their mean. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard
error but does not change the variance of the data.

S5.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
S5.text: 1. Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics summarize a dataset. Measures of central tendency are the mean (the sum of the values divided by the number of values), the median (the middle value of the sorted data) and the mode (the most frequent value). The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is robust to them. For right-skewed data such as incomes the mean is usually larger than the median. Measures of spread describe variability. The range is maximum minus minimum. The variance averages squared deviations from the mean, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it has the same units as the data. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 minus Q1 and is used to flag outliers: a common rule marks values below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 * IQR. S6.text: 4. Sampling and Confidence Intervals A population is the entire group of interest and a sample is a subset used to learn about it. Simple random sampling gives every member an equal chance of selection; stratified sampling samples within subgroups; convenience sampling is easy but prone to bias. Sampling bias occurs when the sample systematically differs from the population. The sampling distribution of the mean describes how sample means vary from sample to sample. The Central Limit Theorem states that for sufficiently large n the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal with mean mu and standard error sigma / sqrt(n), regardless of the shape of the original population.
